history.title: Crew Launch Week 12: The Story of Your Trimester

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Perseverance. "I persevere to produce high quality work."

This week you tell the story of your trimester: one level and one piece of evidence for each HOWL, then one gap, rehearsed for a student-led conference.

1. Read **The Story of Your Trimester** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Claim or Evidence?** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Adjective or Evidence?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is about Zoe and Malik.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [HOWL Tracker](#sel-hub/howlTracker?station=sel_station_crew_launch_story). Open History and the SLC rehearsal tab, and pull one piece of evidence per HOWL from your check-ins and station records. Then open [Strengths Finder](#sel-hub/strengths?station=sel_station_crew_launch_story) to name what you did well in words more specific than "good."
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your three-HOWL story with one gap.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Level, Evidence, Gap**.
9. Finish with the **Explore Challenge: Two Minutes, Three HOWLs**, and rehearse it with a partner.

Your commitment: this week, rehearse your two-minute trimester story with a partner, and take one piece of their feedback into the version you will use at the conference. 🎙

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: The Story of Your Trimester
history.data:
## The Story of Your Trimester

**HOWL: "I persevere to produce high quality work."**

In week 1, your **Crew** wrote norms. Since then you have repaired something, named your zone, built a system, made an ask, rated your own work, asked a question before deciding, made a small move, set a boundary, checked your system after six weeks, and named your part of a whole. Some of it stuck. Some of it did not. All of it is **evidence**.

At an EL school, you tell the story of your learning to someone who matters. At King that includes a **student-led conference** in the fall and in the spring: you, a family member, and your Crew teacher, with a portfolio of your work, and you do the talking. Your **HOWL** grades are on each **trimester** report card. The conference is where you say what is behind them. This week is a **rehearsal**.

The Perseverance HOWL includes **self-assessing** your work with targets and rubrics and learning from feedback. A trimester story is that skill turned on yourself. The target is the HOWL statement. The rubric is the 1 to 4 scale. The evidence is what actually happened, and that is the part that decides whether the story is any good.

Here is a moment from a fictional Crew. Two students rehearse their Responsibility story. Zoe says, "I think I am a 3 because I try hard and I am pretty responsible." Her partner, Malik, says, "I would say a 3. In week 4 I built a launch check and it worked four mornings out of five for two weeks. Then it broke when my schedule changed, and at the six-week check I moved it to after dinner and got five out of five the next week. It is not a 4 because there are still mornings I forget my charger." Both **claim** a 3. Only one of them has told a **believable** story, one a listener could check, because only one of them has a count, a date, and a thing that went wrong.

That is the whole secret of a good trimester story. **Adjectives** are not evidence. "Responsible," "hard-working," and "respectful" are claims. A morning count, a norm you kept on a Tuesday, an ask you made in ELA, a small move at lunch: those are evidence. The best stories also include the part that did not work, because a story with no **gap** in it is a story nobody believes, and because the gap is where next trimester starts.

Your HOWL Tracker has your weekly check-ins, your station records, and your history. Your Strengths Finder can help you name what you actually did well, in words that are more specific than "good." Put them together. Three HOWLs, one **level** each, one piece of evidence each, one gap. Two minutes. Say it to a partner this week. Say it to a family member at the conference. That is what learning from feedback looks like when the feedback is your own.

questions.question: What is a student-led conference, according to the reading?
options: A meeting where the teacher explains your HOWL grades to your family while you listen
A meeting where students in a Crew vote on the norms they want for next trimester
A meeting with a family member and a teacher about your learning, where you do the talking
A meeting where you present your finished expedition product to the whole class

options: The target is the HOWL statement; the rubric is the 1 to 4 scale
The target is the report card; the rubric is your teacher's opinion
The target is a 4; the rubric is how hard you tried
The target is the expedition product; the rubric is the audience's reaction

questions.question: Zoe and Malik both claim a 3. Why is Malik's story the believable one?

Because he has a count, a date, and a thing that went wrong
Because he claims a lower level than he really deserves, to be safe
Because he uses stronger adjectives, like responsible and hard-working

Because a story with no gap is not believed, and the gap is where next trimester starts

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evidence, not adjectives | Three adjectives | One HOWL with real evidence | Every HOWL has a count, a date, or a thing you did |
| The gap | No gap, or "nothing really" | A gap named vaguely | A gap named specifically, with what starts next trimester |
| Rehearsed | Written, not said | Said once to a partner | Said, feedback taken, one thing changed |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if I do not have evidence for a HOWL?
data.answer: Then the honest story is "I do not have a moment I can point to for this one, and that is my gap." That sentence is evidence of self-assessment, which is the Perseverance HOWL doing its job. Then pick the week that would have given you one, and start there.

data.question: What if my level is lower than what I think my teacher will give?
data.answer: Say your level and your evidence anyway. A conference where you claim a 2 with a real story and your teacher says "I saw a 3, here is why" is the best kind. The reverse, a 4 with adjectives, is the worst kind.

data.question: Do I have to talk about the gap in front of my family?
data.answer: Yes, and it is the part families remember best, because it sounds like you. A gap with a plan attached is not a confession. It is the next trimester.

data.question: Two minutes is not very long.
data.answer: Correct. Three HOWLs with a level and one piece of evidence each, one gap, and where next trimester starts: that is five sentences. Two minutes is generous. If it runs long, you have adjectives in it.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Perseverance HOWL says you self-assess with targets and learn from feedback. A trimester story is both, about yourself, out loud. Your teachers score HOWLs; the conference is where you say what is behind the score.

data.title: Two Minutes, Three HOWLs
data.instructions: Build your two-minute trimester story from your HOWL Tracker history and station records: one level and one piece of evidence for each of the three HOWLs, then one gap. Rehearse it with a partner, take one piece of their feedback, and record the version you will use at the conference.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behaviors are self-assessing with targets and rubrics and learning from feedback to revise. The story is the self-assessment; the partner rehearsal is the feedback; the changed version is the revision.

brief.context: You have twelve weeks of check-ins, station records, and moments. Your family will hear about your HOWLs at the conference. Right now the story in your head is probably three adjectives. You are going to replace them with evidence.
brief.role: A student preparing to lead a conference
brief.audience: A partner in Crew first; then a family member and a teacher at the student-led conference
brief.drivingQuestion: What level would I claim for each HOWL, what one moment proves it, and what is my gap?
brief.seedDirection: Open HOWL Tracker History. For each HOWL, find the check-in or station record with the most specific evidence. Write the level and the moment. Pick one gap across all three. Say it to a partner in two minutes. Ask them what was an adjective. Change that one thing.
lockedLessonFacts: The target is the HOWL statement; the rubric is the 1 to 4 scale; the evidence is what actually happened.
Adjectives are claims; a count, a date, or a thing you did is evidence.
A story with no gap is not believed, and the gap is where next trimester starts.
Three HOWLs, one level each, one piece of evidence each, one gap, two minutes.
openQuestions: Which week gave me the strongest evidence for each HOWL?
Is my level one I can back up, or one I hope for?
Which gap is the honest one?
What did my partner hear as an adjective?
stakeholders: A family member at the conference
The teacher who scores the HOWL
criteria: Each HOWL has a level and one piece of evidence with a day, a class, or a count
The story was said aloud to a partner and timed
One thing was changed because of feedback, and the record says what
Uses at least three glossary words
constraints: No adjectives about yourself without a moment attached
Evidence comes from your own records, not from memory alone
brief.deliverable: A one-page story card: three HOWLs with level and evidence, the gap, the next-trimester line, and one sentence on what the partner changed.

parallelExample.context: A fictional student's first draft for Respect was "I am respectful to everyone."
parallelExample.move: Her partner said that was an adjective. She opened her week 8 station record: "At lunch on a Thursday I said 'wait, what happened next' when Tomas got cut off." The level stayed a 3. The sentence changed.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the feedback loop working in one exchange: adjective out, moment in, level unchanged.
